verdicts.claim: By default SQLite runs an automatic checkpoint when a COMMIT makes the WAL 1000 pages or larger (about 4 MB) and when the last connection closes
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages'; 'about 4MB'; 'run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT'; SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT named

verdicts.claim: All automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE ... PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=N sets the threshold; N <= 0 turns auto-checkpointing off
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'Setting the auto-checkpoint size to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off ... All automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE.'

verdicts.claim: PASSIVE copies as many frames as it can without waiting and never calls the busy handler. FULL ... blocks new writers but not readers
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: 'The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode'; FULL 'blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed'; TRUNCATE 'truncates the log file to zero bytes'; NOOP 'always checkpoints zero frames'

verdicts.claim: Every checkpoint takes an exclusive checkpoint lock. If another checkpoint holds it, the call returns SQLITE_BUSY at once and does not call the busy handler
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: 'All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock ... SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked'; busy-handler returns 0 -> 'proceeds ... same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE ... SQLITE_BUSY is returned'

verdicts.claim: PRAGMA journal_size_limit=N (bytes; default -1 = no limit) truncates the WAL to N whenever it resets
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'Each time a transaction is committed or a WAL file resets ... truncated to the limit'; 'The default journal size limit is -1 (no limit)'; 'WAL file is not truncated following a checkpoint ... overwriting is faster than appending'

verdicts.claim: With synchronous=NORMAL the checkpoint is the only operation that syncs, so running checkpoints in a separate thread or process keeps the main writer from blocking on fsync
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation ... the main thread ... will never block on a sync operation'

verdicts.claim: since 3.11.0 the WAL size for one transaction is proportional to the transaction
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself.'

verdicts.claim: The only safe way to remove a leftover WAL is to open the database with sqlite3_open() and close it again
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'The only safe way to remove a WAL file is to open the database file using one of the sqlite3_open() interfaces then immediately close the database using sqlite3_close().'

verdicts.claim: WAL-reset bug likely present from 3.7.0 (2010) through 3.51.2. SQLite fixed it in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13), with backports 3.44.6 and 3.50.7
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'likely present in all version of SQLite from 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). It is fixed in version 3.51.3 (2026-03-13) and later. Backports ... 3.44.6 and 3.50.7.'

verdicts.claim: theconsensus.dev names SQLite 3.53.0 as the fixed release; WAL page lists three subtypes and once misnames RESTART as RESET
verdicts.evidence: consensus: 'the version built against SQLite 3.53.0 (where the bug is fixed)'; wal.html: 'on FULL and RESET checkpoints.' (framing of 3.53.0 as 'the fixed release' is an interpretation; blog only says fixed in 3.53.0)
